topic.subject: science
topic.title: Transportation in animals and plants
topic.scope: blood, heart, arteries and veins, heartbeat and pulse, excretion, xylem, phloem, transpiration

misconceptions.statement: Deoxygenated blood inside our veins is blue in color.
misconceptions.why: Veins appear blue through the skin and diagrams often use blue to represent deoxygenated blood.
misconceptions.fix: Human blood is always red; deoxygenated blood is just a darker shade of red. It looks blue through skin due to how light interacts with tissue.

probe.question: If you were to see blood inside a vein before it touches air, what color would it be?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you see is the only reality

misconceptions.statement: All arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and all veins carry carbon dioxide-rich blood.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the primary function of the systemic circuit.
misconceptions.fix: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it towards the heart. The pulmonary artery carries CO2-rich blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries O2-rich blood to the heart.

probe.question: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?

misconceptions.statement: The heart is the organ where blood is actually created.
misconceptions.why: The heart is the central organ of the system, leading to the belief it is the source of the fluid itself.
misconceptions.fix: The heart only pumps blood; blood cells are actually produced in the bone marrow of certain bones.

probe.question: Where are new red blood cells made in the human body?

misconceptions.root_belief: one organ does everything for a system

misconceptions.statement: Pulse and heartbeat are two completely different and unrelated processes.
misconceptions.why: Students feel the pulse in the wrist and the heartbeat in the chest, perceiving them as separate events.
misconceptions.fix: The pulse is the direct result of the heartbeat; every time the heart pumps blood into the arteries, it creates a throb called a pulse.

probe.question: If your heart rate increases, what happens to your pulse rate?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays the same because they are different

misconceptions.statement: Excretion and egestion are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Both involve removing waste from the body, leading to linguistic and conceptual blurring.
misconceptions.fix: Excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes (like urea in urine) from the blood, while egestion is the removal of undigested food as faeces.

probe.question: Is passing stool (faeces) an example of excretion in the biological sense?

misconceptions.root_belief: all waste removal is the same process

misconceptions.statement: Plants 'suck' water up through the xylem like a person using a straw.
misconceptions.why: Students apply human-centric mechanical actions to biological processes they cannot see.
misconceptions.fix: Water moves up due to transpiration pull, a physical force created by evaporation from leaves, and capillary action, not active sucking.

probe.question: What provides the main force to move water to the top of a tall tree?
probe.wrong_answer: The plant sucks it up using energy

misconceptions.statement: Food in plants only moves downwards from the leaves to the roots.
misconceptions.why: Gravity and the fact that leaves are usually 'up' lead to the belief that transport is unidirectional.
misconceptions.fix: Phloem transports food in both upward and downward directions to reach all parts of the plant, including growing buds and storage organs.

probe.question: In spring, how does stored sugar move from roots to new growing buds?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot move upwards in the phloem

misconceptions.statement: Transpiration is a waste of water and has no benefit to the plant.
misconceptions.why: Students see water loss as inherently negative for survival.
misconceptions.fix: Transpiration creates the suction pull needed to transport water and minerals and also helps in cooling the plant.

probe.question: What would happen to water transport if a plant stopped transpiring?
probe.wrong_answer: It would improve because water is saved

misconceptions.statement: The kidneys produce urine directly from the food we eat in the stomach.
misconceptions.why: Students lack a clear understanding of the blood's role as an intermediary in transport.
misconceptions.fix: Kidneys filter waste from the blood; the food must first be digested and absorbed into the blood before wastes reach the kidneys.

probe.question: How does waste from your cells reach the kidneys?

misconceptions.root_belief: connected systems are one single pipe

misconceptions.statement: The left and right sides of the heart are connected so blood can flow between them.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the heart is one big hollow bag rather than a partitioned pump.
misconceptions.fix: The heart has a wall called the septum that completely separates the left and right sides to prevent mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

probe.question: What prevents oxygen-rich blood from mixing with carbon dioxide-rich blood in the heart?
probe.wrong_answer: The blood knows which way to go

misconceptions.root_belief: an organ is a simple container

misconceptions.statement: Roots 'search' for water in the soil and grow towards it intentionally.
misconceptions.why: Attributing human-like intentions and senses to plants.
misconceptions.fix: Roots grow in all directions; they simply grow more successfully and branch more in areas where they happen to encounter moisture.

probe.question: How do roots find water deep in the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: They sense where it is and turn towards it

misconceptions.statement: Blood is mostly made of red blood cells and contains very little liquid.
misconceptions.why: The name 'blood' and its red appearance make students focus on the cells rather than the medium.
misconceptions.fix: More than half of the blood (about 55%) is actually a straw-colored liquid called plasma.

probe.question: What is the largest component of human blood by volume?

misconceptions.root_belief: the most visible part is the largest part
